summary:
Mars Outpost Manager: Sol 1 to Sol 100 is a free browser game where students run a four-person Mars outpost for 100 sols. Each turn, players place solar arrays, oxygen generators, greenhouses, water recyclers, and radiation shields. They must keep power, oxygen, water, food, and crew health in balance while dust storms, solar flares, leaks, and equipment failures test their plans.

It meets the challenge by making real engineering trade-offs tangible and fun. Life support gets power first, shielding costs credits that could fund a farm, and every decision has a visible consequence. A final report explains what caused the mission’s success or failure and links each cause to a real NASA fact.

The game uses NASA data. Radiation is calibrated to Curiosity’s measured surface dose of 0.67 mSv per sol, the oxygen generator is modeled on MOXIE, water recycling is capped at the ISS’s 98% recovery, and storms reflect Opportunity’s loss in 2018. Mars missions fail or succeed on resource balance, and this game lets students feel that for themselves.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Mars Outpost Manager: Sol 1 to Sol 100 is a browser-based game where the player commands a four-person Mars outpost for 100 sols (Martian days). Each sol, the player allocates limited resources across power, oxygen, water, food, life support and radiation shielding. Every decision affects the others. For example, diverting power to shielding leaves less for oxygen generation, and random events such as dust storms, equipment failures and shortages force the player to adapt. The game ends after sol 100 or when the crew can no longer survive, and an end report summarizes how the outpost performed and why.

What benefits does it have?

  • Players learn the real trade-offs of off-world survival by experiencing them, not by reading about them.
  • It builds systems thinking, prioritization and risk management in a short, replayable session.
  • It runs in any browser with no installation, so it is easy to use in classrooms or at home.

What is the intended impact?

We want to make space science approachable and exciting for students. By turning the constraints of a Martian outpost into a game, we hope to spark interest in STEM and space exploration, and to show that sustaining human life on another planet is a balancing problem, not a single technical fix.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did we use?

  • [Languages/framework: e.g., HTML, CSS, JavaScript / React / Next.js, fill in your actual stack]
  • GitHub for version control and team collaboration
  • Vercel for deployment and hosting
  • [Design/AI tools, if any: e.g., Figma, Claude for development help]
  • Hardware: standard laptops, no special hardware required to play

How is the project creative?

  • It frames resource management as a story. The player is a commander with a crew’s lives at stake, not just managing numbers.
  • Random events keep every playthrough different, so there is no single winning formula.
  • The end report turns each run into a lesson, showing the player which choices led to success or failure.
  • It was built by four CSE students who care about both engineering and education.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Educational value: the resources and events reflect real challenges of Mars missions.
  • Balance and fairness: the game should be challenging but winnable, with meaningful decisions each sol.
  • Accessibility: it works in a browser with simple controls and no setup.
  • Reliability: it needed to run without errors and deploy cleanly on Vercel and GitHub.
  • Scope and time: we chose a focused top-down design over a complex simulation so we could polish it and finish on time.
  • Replayability: random events and varied outcomes encourage players to try again and improve.
